deep.reconstruction:
This is a sketch page with almost no text. The context (cote 80, 'Systèmes de pseudo-droites') points to arrangements of lines and pseudo-lines in the real projective plane, lifted to arrangements of great circles (pseudo-circles) on S².

(1) Top-left: a sphere crossed by great circles meeting at marked points. This is the lift of a projective line arrangement to S² via the double cover S² → RP².

(2) Grid (left middle): a square grid of lines with vertices marked alternately by dots and crosses. This is a 2-colouring of the vertices of a line arrangement, or a local picture of one.

(3) Cube-related polyhedra:
- Bottom left: a cube cut by the three coordinate planes. This is the cell structure given by 3 great circles, i.e. the octahedral subdivision of S².
- Blue figure: an octahedron, or a rhombohedral view of a cube, with inner tetrahedral or star structure. It is labelled '4' (overwritten with 3 or 5).
- Bottom right: a cube with a polyhedron whose vertices sit at the edge midpoints, apparently a cuboctahedron.
- Upper middle: a pyramidal sketch.

(4) Computations:
- '48 = 2·4!'. This is the order of the full octahedral group B₃ ≅ S₄ × Z/2. It is also the automorphism group of the arrangement of 4 great circles in general position on S². That arrangement is the cuboctahedral cell decomposition: its symmetries permute the 4 circles arbitrarily (S₄), and the antipodal map adds a factor of 2. Equivalently, the unique simple arrangement of 4 lines in RP² has automorphism group S₄.
- '12 = 8×3×2/4'. This counts the vertices of that cuboctahedron: 8 triangles × 3 edges gives 24 edges (each edge borders exactly one triangle); ×2 endpoints, ÷ vertex degree 4, gives 12 vertices. As a check, C(4,2)·2 = 12 intersection points on S².
- '5!/(2·4!) = 5/2'. The analogous attempt for 5 lines. The non-integer result shows that the naive guess (a symmetric group times 2 acting on a single type) fails for 5 lines. Indeed, simple arrangements of 5 lines are not unique, and the regular pentagonal one has only dihedral symmetry D₅.
- '3×2×3' next to a branching tree. This is an enumeration tree counting combinatorial choices, presumably isomorphism types of cell configurations or labellings when adding lines.

The next page labels cells q₁…q₆ with numbers 3, 2, 5 (polygon sizes of cells), which supports reading this as an enumeration of small arrangements.

The page serves the elementary groundwork of the pseudo-line project: understanding small arrangements, their spherical lifts, and their symmetry groups.
errors: '5!/(2·4!) = 5/2' is arithmetically correct (120/48), but as a count it is meaningless (non-integer). It is presumably a quick check showing that the 4-line pattern (symmetry 2·n!) does not extend to n = 5, not an error in the strict sense.

ideas.what: Lift of projective line arrangements to great-circle arrangements on S², with polyhedral cell structures (octahedron for 3 circles, cuboctahedron for 4)
ideas.modern_name: Zonotopal / central hyperplane arrangements in R³; oriented matroids of rank 3
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Steiner, Levi 1926, Grünbaum 1972; Folkman–Lawrence 1978 for oriented matroids)

ideas.what: Automorphism group of the simple 4-line arrangement: |Aut| = 2·4! = 48 on the sphere, i.e. the octahedral group
ideas.modern_name: Symmetry group of the cuboctahedron / B₃ Coxeter group

ideas.what: Euler-type counting of vertices/edges/faces of an arrangement cell complex (12 = 8·3·2/4)

ideas.modern_name: Enumeration of simple arrangements / isomorphism types of pseudo-line arrangements

deep.surprise_reason: Exploratory sketches and elementary counts (the octahedral group of order 48, the cuboctahedron as the arrangement of 4 great circles). These are classical facts; nothing new or uncredited is visible, though the page documents Grothendieck's hands-on starting point for the pseudo-line project.
transcription_corrections: Top formula '48 = 2.4!': the leading digit appears overwritten (4 over 1).
The second formula reads '5!/(2.4!) = 5/2'; the right-hand side is faint.
The isolated '4' next to the blue polyhedron is overwritten with another digit (looks like 3 or 5), not a plain 4.
'3×2×3' is written diagonally beside a branching tree diagram and a wavy curve; the tree is a drawing, not text.
'11' at bottom left is the page number.
The transcription omits all the drawings: sphere with great circles, dotted/crossed grid, pyramid, blue octahedron/cube, subdivided cube, cube with inscribed cuboctahedron.
